claim: Plimsoll runs untrusted code, such as code written by an AI agent, inside a sandbox. Every result reports how strong the sandbox was, and a request can demand a minimum strength. If the sandbox is weaker, nothing runs.
quote: plimsoll runs untrusted code, such as code an AI agent wrote, inside a sandbox, and every result says how strong that sandbox was. A request can demand a minimum strength; if the sandbox is weaker, nothing runs.

claim: The name comes from the Plimsoll line, the load-limit mark on a ship's hull. There are four tiers, from weakest to strongest: process, container, kernel, vm.
quote: The name comes from the Plimsoll line, the load limit painted on the outside of a ship's hull where anyone can check it. plimsoll does the same for the isolation tier: how strong the wall around a run is, stated as one of four levels, weakest first: process, container, kernel, vm.

claim: A request below the floor is refused before any code runs. The error means nothing ran.
quote: Every request can set a floor, and a request whose floor the daemon cannot meet is refused before any code runs: ErrInsufficientIsolation means nothing ran.

claim: In the source, the floor check runs immediately before admission and dispatch. A request with no floor set (Unknown) passes without a check, so the per-request floor is opt-in.
quote: Call it immediately before admission and dispatch so a stale discovery/readiness result can never authorize a run. ... if minimum == IsolationUnknown { return nil }

claim: Plimsoll does not build the isolation itself. That is delegated to gVisor and Firecracker, and Plimsoll is the gatekeeping and reporting layer in front of them.
quote: Isolation itself is delegated to gVisor and Firecracker. This project is the layer in front of them that decides which requests may run and reports the evidence; it does not implement a sandbox boundary of its own and does not claim to.

claim: The tier is evidence the daemon collects from its configuration and startup checks. It is not cryptographic attestation.
quote: The tier is evidence the daemon collected: its configuration and its own startup checks. It is not attestation, cryptographic proof from the hardware of what software is running, and no provider here offers that.

claim: The VM tier for E2B is inferred from which provider is configured, not measured. A compromised Docker daemon or E2B control plane would defeat the evidence.
quote: A compromised Docker daemon, or an E2B control plane (the E2B servers that create and manage the microVMs) that did not do what it says, defeats the evidence. Treat the tier as this daemon's observation, not as remote attestation.

claim: The project is pre-1.0 with a single author and no external users. It has never had a third-party security audit.
quote: Pre-1.0, single author, no external users yet. Breaking changes land without a deprecation path, on purpose. No third-party security audit has ever been performed

claim: The author's motivating example was a popular embeddable JavaScript sandbox that advertised a MemoryLimit which did nothing.
quote: a popular embeddable JavaScript sandbox advertised a MemoryLimit that did nothing. The library promised a limit it did not enforce, and nothing in its types or its docs revealed that.

claim: The author checked six hosted sandbox services in September 2026 (author's claim) and says none returned the isolation level a run actually got or refused runs below a stated minimum.
quote: None of them returns the wall a run actually got, and none refuses a run that would get less than a minimum the caller stated.

claim: Northflank says it uses gVisor where nested virtualisation is unavailable. That is the situation Plimsoll cites: the isolation a run gets depends on the host it lands on.
quote: with gVisor applied where syscall-interception isolation is sufficient or where nested virtualisation is unavailable.

claim: gVisor intercepts application system calls and acts as the guest kernel. That is the basis of Plimsoll's 'kernel' tier.
quote: intercepts application system calls and acts as the guest kernel

claim: The author's measurements found that Docker accepts --pids-limit under every runtime, but Kata did not apply it (200 of 200 processes started at a limit of 64). Under gVisor the limit is applied on the host, and the guest got only 14 processes at a limit of 64.
quote: Kata max 200 of 200 no limit at all ... At a limit of 64 the guest got 14 processes.

claim: The Kata issue about the PIDs limit not reaching the guest was closed as not planned.
quote: It seems there is no way to provide this value to the agent, so that it is put in place in the guest.

claim: On a self-hosted setup, the strongest wall is gVisor. The VM tier is available only through E2B or Docker Cloud, which bill by the second. gVisor roughly doubled the time of a TypeScript compile-and-run in the author's measurement.
quote: Self-hosted, its strongest boundary is gVisor (it reports that as the kernel tier). The VM tier comes only from E2B or Docker Cloud Sandboxes, which bill by the second. ... a one-file TypeScript compile-and-run took 4.1 s under gVisor against 1.95 s as a plain container

claim: The author describes Plimsoll as a Go daemon whose backend is switched through configuration, so code that needs a VM cannot quietly run on a test setup.
quote: Every result states its isolation tier (process, container, kernel or vm), and a request can set a minimum, so code that needs a VM can't quietly run on my test setup: below the floor, nothing runs.

claim: The author lists the project's limits on HN: no other users, no outside audit, a bus factor of one, and on a Mac only the container tier, because gVisor is Linux-only.
quote: What it isn't yet: pre-1.0, no other users, no outside security audit, and it's just me: the bus factor is one, and I'm careful around buses. gVisor is Linux only, so a Mac gets the container tier.

claim: The only HN community reply asked whether a remote SSH sandbox (exe.dev) plus a credential-injecting proxy would be enough. The author answered that Plimsoll is for running code for agents, not for running the agents themselves.
quote: plimsoll is more for running code for agents or MCP servers. It's not for running agents.

claim: Agent code can call an API through a broker that sits outside the sandbox. The broker checks the exact route and attaches a credential minted for that run, and the credential never enters the sandbox.
quote: The credential is minted per run: plimsoll asks for it once per run, so it can be a fresh short-lived token, and it never enters the sandbox.

claim: By the project's own statement, a grant is also a way for data to leave: the broker checks the method and route but not what the call carries.
quote: Every grant is also a way out for data. The broker ... checks each call's method and route against the grant, never what the call carries.

claim: The repo showed 25 stars and 1 fork when fetched on 2026-10-14.
quote: 25 stars ... 1 fork
